results.content: S-EPMC2394553 - When individual behaviour matters: homogeneous and network models in epidemiology. ### Dataset Information ### When individual behaviour matters: homogeneous and network models in epidemiology. In recent years, several network-based approaches have been developed to explicitly model heterogeneity in host contact patterns. We then evaluate a variety of methodologies for incorporating contact heterogeneity, including network-based models and several modifications to the simple SIR compartmental model. In general, however, network models are more intuitive and accurate for predicting disease spread through heterogeneous host populations. ### Publications ### When individual behaviour matters: homogeneous and network models in epidemiology. In recent years, several network-based approaches have been developed to explicitly model heterogeneity in host contact patterns. **Project description:**Often, when modeling infectious disease spread, the complex network through which the disease propagates is approximated by simplified spatial information. Here, we simulate epidemic spread through various contact networks and fit spatial-based models in a Bayesian framework using Markov chain Monte Carlo methods. Spatial models tend to predict infection probability reasonably well when disease spread is propagated through contact networks in which contacts are only within a certain distance of each other. Here we explore this potential by showing how combining two modelling approaches (social network analysis, SNA, and agent-based modelling, ABM) could lead to more robust insights into a particular type of conservation intervention. We use our simple model, which simulates knowledge of ranger patrols through a hunting community and is based on empirical data from a Cambodian protected area, to highlight the complex, context-dependent nature of outcomes of information-sharing interventions, depending both on the configuration of the network and the attributes of the agents. **Project description:**Infectious disease transmission between individuals in a heterogeneous population is often best modelled through a contact network. Here, we consider the fit of an individual level model containing a spatially-based contact network that is either entirely, or partially, unobserved within a Bayesian framework, using data augmented Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC). We also examine the performance of the data augmented MCMC analysis in the presence or absence of contact network observational models based upon either knowledge about the degree distribution or the total number of connections in the network.

results.title: An In-Depth Look at New Network Contagion Models
results.content: # An In-Depth Look at New Network Contagion Models. In recent years, the study of network contagion models has revolutionized our understanding of how events, shocks, or innovations propagate through complex economic systems. ### Defining Network Contagion Models. At its core, a network contagion model is a mathematical framework that simulates the spread of an entity—be it information, risk, or a financial shock—across interconnected nodes. Network contagion models provide the theoretical underpinning to analyze and prevent such systemic failures. A foundational mathematical approach in network contagion models is the use of differential equations and probability theory to capture the dynamics of contagion. Graph theory offers a potent set of tools to model the topology of financial networks. * **Simplification of Complex Realities:** Often, the models require simplifying assumptions—such as homogeneous mixing of nodes or constant contagion rates—that may not fully capture the heterogeneous nature of real economic networks. Network contagion models have found a wide array of applications in economics, particularly in understanding market dynamics, systemic risk, and regulatory implications. * **Systemic Risk Assessment:** Network models help pinpoint “too interconnected to fail” institutions, guiding regulators in prioritizing oversight and implementing safeguards. Several case studies underscore the practical utility of network contagion models:. The insights gained from network contagion models inform both national and international regulatory frameworks. Research in network contagion models is rapidly evolving. * **Multilayer Networks:** Incorporating multiple layers of interaction (e.g., financial transactions, trade, and information flows) into a single model can provide a more holistic view of economic dynamics. Network contagion models have emerged as a powerful tool in the modern economist’s arsenal. By applying techniques from graph theory, stochastic processes, and data analytics, these models illuminate how localized disturbances can cascade into systemic crises—an insight critical for effective risk management and policy design. By staying informed about the latest advancements in network contagion models, stakeholders can better anticipate financial turbulence, design more resilient systems, and ultimately contribute to a more stable global economy. This in-depth exploration of network contagion models not only underscores their theoretical foundations and practical applications but also highlights the indispensable role of cutting-edge research and technology in shaping the future of economic modeling.

Title: Improving tobacco social contagion models using agent-based simulations on networks | Applied Network Science | Springer Nature Link
One reason why social contagion is often dismissed is that existing models of smoking dynamics tend to be based on ordinary differential equation (ODE), which are not fit to study the impact of network effects on smoking dynamics. Over the years, the effect of social networks on individual and population behaviour have been studied in both opinion dynamics and epidemiology (Rahmandad and Sterman 2008 Heterogeneity and network structure in the dynamics of diffusion: comparing agent-based and differential equation models. Additionally, we show that ABMs on fully connected networks and ODE models should not be used to model smoking behaviour as they replicate the real-world data with poor accuracy compared to the other networks. We estimate two parameters for our model based on the results from the FHS data-related network analysis (Christakis and Fowler 2008 The collective dynamics of smoking in a large social network. Additionally, we impose the values of two parameters (\(\beta \_{N,S\rightarrow S,S}\) and \(\beta \_{S,Q \rightarrow Q,Q}\)) of the model by estimating them from empirical research (Christakis and Fowler 2008 The collective dynamics of smoking in a large social network. This suggests that a simple traditional ODE model can be used to model smoking behaviour and other similar social contagions only when the local population under study follows a fully-connected network topology. Additionally, the ABM on FC networks gives the worst fit to the validation data and the least number of successful crossovers showing that the ABM on FC networks and, by extension, ODE models should not be used to model smoking and similar behavioural contagion. We have developed an agent-based model for smoking dynamics that considers the contagious nature of smoking behaviour by including network effects. Importantly, given the difficulties in collecting data on offline social networks, we find that the LFR and ER network replicates the empirical data with accuracy and also their calibrated parameter values are not significantly different from those of the FHS network, suggesting that the LFR and ER networks can be used for social contagion models of tobacco use.
